storm.summary_layperson: A weak-to-moderate storm cell (35–39 dBZ) has closed to within 3 miles west-northwest of the cove and, by radar timing, may already be arriving — but Riverside YC and the Old Greenwich waterfront station aren't picking up any rain yet, so it's close without being confirmed overhead. The Sound isn't offering any protective buffer tonight, so whatever does arrive won't be weakened crossing the water.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Water (75.0°F) and air (75.2°F) are within 0.2°F of each other right now and stay that way through the whole evening per the hourly trend — there's no marine layer standing by tonight to choke incoming storms.
storm.detail_html:
The NWS forecast for this period carries a 90% chance of showers and thunderstorms, and the OKX Area Forecast Discussion is explicit: a severe thunderstorm watch is active until midnight for NYC metro, NE New Jersey, and the Lower Hudson Valley, with "the main threat for severe thunderstorm development... now through about 9pm" — squarely inside this window. That said, a point-specific check of active NWS alerts for Riverside/Greenwich itself comes back empty, so the watch as issued does not currently cover this exact location, even though the AFD's broader threat language clearly does.

KOKX radar shows the nearest tracked cells 2.4–2.9 miles WNW of the cove at 35–39 dBZ, closing at roughly 38 kt. Farther out, two stronger cells (52–53 dBZ) sit 29–31 miles to the W/WSW, with several more scattered out to 45 miles. Instability is moderate (CAPE 1,140 J/kg, HRRR f01) but 0–6 km shear is unusually strong — 38 kt now, forecast to climb to 55–59 kt over the next couple hours — exactly the kind of organization the AFD's severe language is keying on, even though nothing at the cove itself has reached severe criteria yet.

The arrival-prediction engine flags the nearest cell as technically overdue, but that ETA leans on a system-wide radar-centroid motion estimate (41.3 kt / 47 mph) that measures the whole reflectivity field's drift, not this specific cell's own propagation speed — it can run fast when the broader system is reorganizing rather than translating as a unit. Ground truth backs up some skepticism: RYC's rain rate reads 0.0 in/hr and the Old Greenwich waterfront APRS station shows 0.0 mm of rain in the last hour, both as of the past few minutes. Read this as imminent-to-arriving, not confirmed-overhead — worth stepping outside and checking the sky rather than trusting the ETA math alone.

There's no local buffer working in the cove's favor tonight. Water and air are essentially the same temperature (75.0°F vs 75.2°F, a 0.2°F gap) and the hourly projection keeps it that way — or lets air temperature fall below water — through the rest of the window and overnight. The marine layer mechanism that sometimes chokes incoming storms crossing the Sound simply isn't present; anything that reaches the cove arrives at whatever strength it had approaching the water.

What would change this call: either of the 52–53 dBZ cells to the W/WSW accelerating toward the cove instead of holding their current track, the severe thunderstorm watch expanding to cover the CT shore, or RYC/the Old Greenwich station starting to report rain or a gust spike in the next 15–30 minutes.

wind.tactics_blurb: RYC now: ENE 70° at 3.4 kt, gusting 12 (10-min avg 7.4) — light gradient wind, no sea breeze building tonight (air–water gap only 0.2°F, well under the 5°F thermal gate). A storm cell tracking just WNW of the cove could bring a squally jump in speed and a backing shift over the next hour before conditions settle into steadier ENE-to-NE gradient flow in the 12–15 kt range through the middle of the window, then ease back to 8–10 kt after 9 PM. Favor the center of the course early given the storm-driven uncertainty; once the NE settles in, pressure should run fairly even across the cove.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
DeltaT is only 0.2°F right now — water and air are essentially the same temperature — nowhere near the 5°F gate this framework requires for a thermal sea breeze, and the station network confirms it: only 5% of coastal stations are reading southerly and the sea-breeze active flag is false. That makes tonight a gradient-only day, not a sea-breeze day. The authoritative airport-network gradient reads 6.8 kt, which lands in the light bucket (light gradient wind — no sea breeze, direction may wander, internally "B-light"): raceable but thin, and per this framework's own flag for exactly that, direction agreement across the 28-station ensemble is a middling 0.61 tonight — the regional wind field is somewhat unsettled on its own, independent of the nearby storm.

RYC right now reads ENE 70° at 3.4 kt (10-min avg 7.4 kt, gusting 11.8) — close enough in direction to HRRR's forecast (ENE 78°) that no divergence flag is warranted, and since tonight isn't a sea-breeze day the maturation correction this framework applies on Regime A/A+ days doesn't come into play regardless.

The hourly table isn't a clean gradient hold tonight — speed builds from 8 kt to a 15 kt peak around 8 PM before easing back to 8–10 kt late, with direction backing steadily from ENE toward NE the whole way. That pattern lines up with the nearby storm cell and the strong 0–6 km shear (38–59 kt through the evening per HRRR) rather than anything thermal — there's no sea breeze here to oscillate, so treat this as a persistent, storm-influenced shift rather than tactical shifts to play. Once the NE settles in for the back half of the window, that's the cleanest direction this cove sees — laminar and steady, with maybe slightly more pressure mid-cove than tight against either shore per the geography table.

In racing terms: the first hour sits in drifter-to-light range (8 kt), building into the 12–15 kt powered-up range with gusts near 18–20 kt through the middle of the window — solid one-design racing if the storm stays clear of the course — before easing back to 8–10 kt after 9 PM. Favor the center of the course early while direction is backing and the storm's exact path is still resolving; once NE settles in, pressure should even out. The bigger variable tonight isn't the wind number — it's whether the nearby storm cell (see the storm section) crosses the course; a lightning call would override this wind forecast entirely.

data_caveats: Nearest tracked storm cell (2.4–2.9 mi WNW, 35–39 dBZ) reads as overdue on the arrival-prediction engine, but its closing speed comes from a system-wide radar-centroid motion estimate (41.3 kt), not a per-cell propagation measurement — ground truth at RYC and the Old Greenwich APRS station shows no rain as of the last few minutes, so treat the overdue flag with caution and watch the sky directly.

No active NWS watch or warning is on file for the Riverside/Greenwich point specifically, even though the OKX Area Forecast Discussion references a severe thunderstorm watch for the broader NYC metro / NE NJ / Lower Hudson Valley region through midnight.
No marine-layer buffer tonight — water (75.0°F) and air (75.2°F) are within 0.2°F of each other and the hourly trend keeps it that way through the rest of the window.
